How the proof fits together

Degrees 2–5

Fourth-moment estimate

Reflection excludes an interior failure throughout this range. Degree five is also covered by the finite argument.

Degrees 5–256

The 15,138-box cover

The near-one radius, reflection and the two-segment contour give the exclusion tests. Exact moments justify the bounds used by the arithmetic witnesses.

Degrees 257 and above

Variance exclusion

The uniform phase estimate controls the variance term. Reflection and the contour inequality then exclude the interior case.

Combine all degrees→Sendov’s theorem and the equality case

Control applications A pole near each marked pole leads to derivative feedback. For the oscillator the two fixed designs yield joint stability radii and a gain crossover.

Separate result A sufficient spectral criterion gives the strict quadratic bound under an additional transverse-energy hypothesis.

The theoremKernel checked

Sendov’s theorem

For a complex polynomial of degree at least two with all roots in the closed unit disk, each root has a critical point at distance at most one.

Explore roots and critical points for a polynomial of your choice.

Hypotheses

Fix a complex polynomial p of degree n ≥ 2, with all roots in |z| ≤ 1, and one of its roots a.

Mathematical result

The stronger result is a lower bound of one on the mean of |a − c|⁻² over the n − 1 critical points c, counted with multiplicity. A critical point at a gives an infinite mean. Equality occurs precisely in the regular boundary configuration. Outside it the distance can be made strictly less than one.

The theoremKernel checked

From a polynomial to reciprocal data

A hypothetical failure of the strict quadratic bound gives one set of reciprocal displacements for all subsequent estimates.

Hypotheses

Rotate an interior marked root to 0 < a < 1 and normalize the leading coefficient. Suppose a is simple and the reciprocal quadratic sum over the critical points is at most N = n − 1.

Mathematical result

Write yⱼ = 1/(a − cⱼ), s = Σyⱼ/N, m = |s|, and q = |1 − as|. The same family gives the origin bound, the lower bound for the reflected integral and the variance bound V ≤ 1 − m². Boundary equality is treated separately.

Low degrees and the sharp fourth power

One fourth-moment inequality covers every positive real exponent up to four.

Hypotheses

Use the scalar reflected envelope Qₐ(t) = a + (1 − a²)t on 0 ≤ t ≤ 1, where 0 ≤ a < 1.

Mathematical result

The integral of Qₐ(t)⁴ is strictly less than one. Interpolation gives the inequality for 0 < p ≤ 4, covering degrees 2–5. For every p > 4 an explicit interior mark gives an integral greater than one, establishing the exact range of this envelope.

A uniform near-one radius

One increasing function specifies a region that cannot contain normalized interior data.

Hypotheses

Take N ≥ 4 and q = |1 − as|. Put R(N) = (1 − 2/N)(1 − 4/(N + 1))²/8.

Mathematical result

If q ≤ min(1/64, R(N)), the centered-product bound and the first-coefficient inequality force a = 1. This contradicts the interior mark. The radius reaches the cap 1/64 from N = 7 (degree 8).

One phase estimate for §§3–4

A single inequality bounds the same exponential integral in the contour argument and the large-degree argument.

Hypotheses

For L ≥ 9 let B(L) = L² ∫₀¹ u² exp[−L(u − u²/2)] du.

Mathematical result

The shared bound is L B(L) ≤ 4 + 18/L ≤ 6. Section 3 uses the first inequality to control the first contour segment. Section 4 uses the bound by six in the variance exclusion.

The two-segment contour

A comparison on the two path segments links the bound at the origin to the reciprocal mean and variance.

Hypotheses

Use the normalized interior data and its common quadratic bound. Compare the product along the path with the diagonal product obtained by replacing every reciprocal displacement by its mean.

Mathematical result

The two segment errors are estimated separately. Their sum gives an inequality for the location of the marked root. Its finite-degree form supplies the necessary origin inequality used by the box tests.

Large degrees

For N ≥ 256, reflection and the two-segment inequality contradict the putative quadratic budget.

How the 15,138 boxes cover the domain

One counted certificate covers degrees 5–256 and all admissible values of the marked radius and reciprocal mean.

Hypotheses

Start with the integer degrees from 5 to 256 and the full closed unit square for a and m. A spatial split covers its common boundary. A degree split gives consecutive integer intervals.

Mathematical result

Each leaf carries a proof of its exclusion. A split combines the two child certificates and adds their leaf counts. The resulting theorem has type CertifiedCount Good rootCube 15138. Coverage and the physical leaf bounds then give a contradiction for every admissible interior polynomial in the finite range.

Assembling the proof in every degree

The finite and large-degree exclusions close the normalized interior proof and recover the theorem for arbitrary complex coefficients.

Hypotheses

Use the low-degree and center arguments, the boundary equality characterization, the finite exclusion for n ≤ 256 and the analytic exclusion for n ≥ 257.

Mathematical result

The contradiction gives the strict alternative outside the regular boundary case. Combining that alternative with the equality case gives the reciprocal quadratic inequality and Sendov’s closed-unit-disk conclusion.

Exact finite verificationKernel checked

Exact rational moments

One recurrence computes the weighted integrals of nonnegative integer powers of a rational quadratic.

Hypotheses

Write Q(t) = A(1 − t)² + Bt(1 − t) + Ct² with A, B, C rational. The moment also allows factors tⁱ(1 − t)ʲ. The reflection and origin comparisons impose their respective positivity and order conditions.

Mathematical result

The rational recurrence equals the real integral. Additional Lean lemmas transfer reflection and the early and late origin comparisons to these moments. These comparisons allow a single reflected witness and the two origin moment bounds to be applied throughout each terminal box.

Exact finite verificationKernel and Python checks

Witnesses and arithmetic replay

A deterministic calculation starts from degrees 5–256 and the full square of possible values of a and m. The tree and its witnesses are generated during the run.

Hypotheses

Use exact integer arithmetic, outward rounding, the uniform near-one radius and the rational moment comparisons. The default run uses three rejection tests.

Replay result

Both Python evaluators report 15,138 terminal boxes at maximum depth 45. Of these, 11,399 close by the origin test, 3,428 by reflection and geometry, and 311 by the near-one bound. The second run recomputes the moments by integration by parts within the same search. Lean verifies 21,174 distinct moment inequalities. A bound used in several terminal boxes is proved once and shared between them. The counted cover records 15,138 leaves. The public dependency audit traces this certificate to both the quadratic inequality and the geometric theorem.

Separate criterionKernel checked · separate result

A sufficient spectral criterion

A condition on the reciprocal source roots alone guarantees a strict quadratic inequality for the critical points.

Hypotheses

Take a monic polynomial of degree N + 1 ≥ 3 with a simple mark 0 < a < 1 and the remaining roots bⱼ in the unit disk. Rotate wⱼ = 1/(a − bⱼ) so that their mean is real. Require 3Σ(Im wⱼ)² ≤ Σ|wⱼ|² in that coordinate system.

Mathematical result

The first two power sums of the reciprocal critical displacements are determined by the source power sums. The transverse-energy condition makes their quadratic sum strictly greater than N. The full degree closure treats configurations outside this sufficient condition.

Theorem 2.1 and Corollary 2.2Kernel checked

Variance of the derivative product

Replacing the reciprocal displacements by their average changes the primitive by at most V/[(N − 1)B³], under the positive-envelope condition B > 0.

Argument

Interpolation between the average and the observed values cancels the first-order term. The sum of squared pairwise differences produces the empirical variance. The polynomial evaluation at the origin then gives (V3), the finite bounds (V4) and their eventual form along a sequence.

Corollary 6.1Kernel checked

A derivative pole near each marked pole

If all poles lie in a disk of radius d > 0, every marked pole lies within d of a pole prescribed by the derivative. The mean squared reciprocal displacement is at least 1/d².

Argument

Translate and scale the disk to apply Theorem 1.1, then undo the change of variables. For a simple marked pole the inverse of the shifted compression has spectral norm at least 1/d and Frobenius norm at least √(n − 1)/d. The paper characterizes equality for the scalar bound. Gauss–Lucas supplies separate bounds on the largest pole modulus and the rightmost real part.

Section 6.1All listed results kernel checked

Realizing the derivative by feedback

For a monic polynomial p of degree n and q = p′/n, feedback can assign (z − γ)q as the characteristic polynomial. With output x₂ − γx₁ the transfer reduces to 1/q.

Argument

Adding the polynomial (z − γ)q − p changes the last companion row. The auxiliary pole remains an internal mode. The section also derives mean-coordinate feedback, an additive matrix margin for a normal plant, and a single-output high-gain limit in which n − 1 poles approach the zeros of q.

Section 6.2All listed results kernel checked

Uncertainty in the polynomial coefficients

For independent complex errors in the n nonleading coefficients, the ℓʳ stability radius is d(P)/n¹⁄ᵗ, where d(P) is the minimum of |P| on the unit circle and t is the conjugate exponent.

Argument

Hölder’s inequality bounds the error on the circle. A perturbation with aligned phases attains the boundary value. Zero padding restores the degree after differentiation. This weakly improves the coefficient radius. A first-difference disturbance channel gives an explicit example in which the peak frequency gain increases.

Section 7All listed results kernel checked

Sampling before or after differentiation

For two continuous poles c ± d, the two orders give eᵀᶜ and eᵀᶜ cosh(Td). Their decay rates can differ.

Argument

For distinct real poles the continuous critical point lies to the left of the logarithmically rescaled sampled critical point in each gap. Lean checks this scalar gap argument. The manuscript also cites Bourin’s general compression inequality for the non-strict comparison. For poles with a common real part, distinct sampled phases put the new critical points strictly inside the sampled pole circle. Phase collisions preserve a boundary pole.

Section 7.1All listed results kernel checked

The oscillator and its actuator

The same nominal oscillator is controlled continuously and with a quarter-period zero-order hold. Each feedback assigns the derivative in its own time domain.

Argument

For an actuator multiplier g the continuous loop is Hurwitz for g > −2. The redesigned sampled loop is Schur for 1 − 1/H < g < (1 + H)/(2H), where H = exp(−π). Holding the continuous gain produces a third interval. The section also computes the open- and closed-loop additive matrix margins.

Proposition 7.1Kernel checked

Can both designs use the same gain?

For damping a > 0, frequency ω > 0 and sin(ωT) ≠ 0, only the feedback row (a, ω) simultaneously assigns both derivative poles.

Argument

The continuous target fixes the second gain. The sampled target and the positivity of the second component of the held input then fix the first. The additional poles are 0 and 1, on the respective stability boundaries.

Section 8, equations F1–F2All listed results kernel checked

Stability for a given physical plant

Damping a, frequency ω and actuator gain g are constant for a given plant. Each controller is fixed at its nominal setting, with sampling period T = π/2.

Argument

For each pair (a, ω), recalculate both the transition and the held input. The continuous quadratic requires a positive damping coefficient and positive determinant. In sampled time the three real quadratic Schur inequalities are affine in g. The common gain interval is their intersection over the prescribed plants.

Theorem 8.1Kernel checked

Exact simultaneous stability radii

The largest open cubes about (1, 1, 1) have relative radii 4√2 − 5 ≈ 0.656854 in continuous time and approximately 0.829678 in sampled time.

Argument

The equilibrium determinant first vanishes at an explicitly constructed plant. Sharpness requires both stability throughout the open cube and a boundary plant attaining equality. For the sampled system one must also exclude a crossing at −1 and a crossing by a nonreal conjugate pair.

Theorem 8.2Kernel checked

The gain at which the advantage changes

Let damping and frequency each vary within 1 ± ε, with 0 ≤ ε ≤ 0.2, and increase the positive actuator gain. The two exact upper gains agree once, at ε ≈ 0.102364.

Argument

Below the crossing the continuous controller tolerates the larger gain. Above it the sampled design tolerates the larger gain. At ε = 0.20 the worst sampled frequency is about 1.17525, inside the frequency interval. Checking the corners alone would miss the instability.

Corollary 8.3Kernel checked

An upward drift in frequency

For damping in [0.99, 1.01] and frequency in [1, W], 1 ≤ W ≤ 2.5, the gain limits cross at W ≈ 1.215794.

Argument

The least admissible upper gain occurs at the smallest damping. In each design the worst frequency is the smaller of W and a stationary frequency. Bounds on the other two Schur inequalities are needed throughout the full rectangle.
